summary: Hard general-population numbers for lower-body lifts are scarce; the best anchors are the ACSM/Cooper-style leg-press ratio norms for 20-29 year olds (men ~1.5-2.3 x BW from p10 to p90, women ~1.1-1.8 x BW, on a selectorized machine) and a sample of untrained university students whose back squat averaged ~1.35 x BW for men (89.9 kg, SD 25.5) and ~1.06 x BW for women (59.7 kg, SD 14.8), with coefficients of variation of ~23-28%. Novice men in a NASA study deadlifted only ~0.93-1.0 x BW (76-82 kg), and the 1RM rose ~7% between sessions just from familiarity, so true never-lifted people are probably below the study figures. Military and firefighter groups sit well above untrained people (soldiers' hex-bar 3RM averaged 238 lb for men and 160 lb for women; fire recruits' 3RM deadlift was ~1.56 x BW), so they act as an upper bound for 'general but active' adults. Training studies show untrained people gain 20-40% on squat, leg press and leg extension within 2-3 months, which suggests the untrained median is roughly 0.7-0.8 x a beginner lifter's level. Leg extension, leg curl, hip thrust, lunge and front squat have no usable untrained norms (machine and protocol differences make absolute kg nearly meaningless); for calf raise the only population norm is reps (median single-leg heel raises ~24 men, ~21 women). Female lower-body strength runs about 65-80% of male in absolute terms, with a smaller gap per kg of body weight.
